articles.title: He Asked for More
articles.deck: A bowl of gruel, a five-pound offer, and the hunger missing from an institution’s account.
body: That evening, the workhouse boys have agreed on a plan.
They draw lots. Whoever is chosen must stand up after supper and ask the master for another bowl of gruel.
The lot falls to Oliver.
The nine-year-old approaches with his empty bowl and says the sentence:
Please, sir, I want some more.
## The room’s response
Watch what follows. The response is the subject of this essay.
The master freezes. He turns pale, steadies himself against the copper, and stares at the boy.
His assistants are equally astonished.
Then come the cries. The master strikes Oliver on the head with the ladle, seizes him, and calls for Mr. Bumble.
Bumble rushes into the boardroom to report that Oliver Twist has asked for more.
The assembled gentlemen are aghast.
One gentleman in a white waistcoat declares that the boy will certainly be hanged.
They then advertise a reward of five pounds to anyone willing to take him as an apprentice.
## Why such a great disturbance?
A nine-year-old says he is still hungry.
The result is an institutional crisis.
Why?
Because the portion has already been calculated.
Dickens describes the calculation: three meals of thin gruel a day, an onion twice a week, and half a roll on Sundays.
The board sets the ration.

He also describes its reasoning with devastating composure. These enlightened gentlemen have discovered that the workhouse is a public entertainment for the poor, somewhere to eat and sleep, a tavern that requires no work.
Their answer is to make it unpleasant.
So unpleasant that the poor will prefer hunger outside to admission.
Dickens gives them two alternatives: gradual starvation inside the house, or a quicker starvation outside it.
One of the book’s fiercest sentences arrives in its second chapter.
## It does not require hatred
Here is the central point, different from the impression many readers carry of the novel.
The board need not hate Oliver.
Its members scarcely know him. No strong personal feeling about this particular boy is required.
He is not really what they are discussing.
They are discussing a budget.
The workhouse costs money, supplied by parish rates. Those funds are limited; local tradespeople and property holders pay them.
The question takes this form: how can the greatest number of poor people be dealt with at the lowest cost?
“Dealt with” has two meanings: discourage them from entering, or reduce the cost of those who do enter.
Cutting the food allowance serves both.

Within that budgetary and administrative reasoning, the plan makes sense. Dickens is satirizing, among other things, the treatment of poverty as a management problem associated with the period of the 1834 Poor Law reform.
The gentlemen can regard themselves as conscientiously doing their jobs.
## Where is the problem?
The things entered into the calculation are people.
A board member writing down so many ounces per person per week handles a quantity multiplied by a head count.
Every unit in that head count is a child capable of hunger.
The page does not distinguish the two descriptions.
Once someone becomes one unit among the counted, there is no obvious place for the question of whether this particular child is hungry.
The question has not necessarily been refuted. It has no column.
Oliver’s request is therefore received not as a request but as an entry outside the permitted form.
The calculation has no way to process it.
It becomes an incident.
## Five pounds to take him away
What follows makes the arrangement clearer.
The parish advertises five pounds for anyone who will take Oliver Twist.
Notice the direction in which the money moves.
The person taking the child does not pay. The parish pays that person.
The child is a liability.
Keep him, and the parish must continue providing gruel. Remove him, and a one-time payment closes the account. Five pounds looks cheaper than continued maintenance.
On this ledger he is a negative entry that five pounds can cancel.
The chimney sweep Gamfield comes to claim him. Dickens notes the accusation that Gamfield has beaten three or four boys to death.
The board agrees to the arrangement.
The price is settled at three pounds ten shillings. What finally stops it is not bargaining: a magistrate notices Oliver’s terror, questions him, and refuses to sign the indenture.
A child’s destination has first been put into a bargain over three pounds ten. On this occasion, someone finally stops to look at the child himself.
## The undertaker’s shop
Oliver is eventually taken by the undertaker Sowerberry.
He sleeps beneath the counter, among the coffins.
A detail of this new arrangement is especially cruel.
Sowerberry finds work for him as a funeral mute.
That is an occupation: a figure in the funeral procession whose appearance communicates mourning. Oliver seems ideal because he is small, thin, and melancholy.
His appearance, Sowerberry thinks, will be particularly effective at children’s funerals.
Notice the reasoning.
Something entirely real in Oliver, his hunger and misery, has been discovered to be an asset.
His sorrowful face can earn money.
Once suffering has a use, those profiting from it have less reason to relieve it.
## More than personal cruelty
The horror is not that there is no cruelty. It is that cruelty can accompany the ordinary fulfillment of a role.
Oliver is beaten. The master uses his ladle; Bumble uses his cane. Noah’s bullying is not the whole of the violence.
Yet in the institution’s account, its officers can still say they have fed him according to the stipulated ration.
The board is also willing to send him to Gamfield. A magistrate’s refusal, not the board’s protection, interrupts that arrangement.
People at each stage can describe themselves as performing their assigned work.
Bumble administers the procedure. The master distributes the ration. The board meets over expenditure. Sowerberry conducts his business.
By their separate procedures, they can consider themselves competent.
And a nine-year-old has scarcely known what it is to eat enough.
## His mother
Return briefly to the first chapter.
Oliver’s mother dies in the workhouse after giving birth.
She has been brought in from the street. Nobody knows who she is or where she comes from. She sees the child, kisses him, and dies.
An old workhouse attendant and a doctor are present.
The doctor has first comforted the mother. After her death, before leaving, he examines her left hand and comments on the absence of a wedding ring.
He calls it the old story.
He puts on his gloves and leaves.
Oliver enters the world through an act of classification.
Unmarried, unknown, dead: the file seems complete.
Years later, the attendant will tell of something else. The dying woman held her hand, spoke to her, and entrusted an object to her care.
The attendant stole that keepsake and later pawned it. At her own death she leaves the pawn ticket.
What the woman said has had no place in the official account of her.
## Next
Oliver eventually runs away.
He leaves the undertaker, walks for seven days toward London, and is nearly starving when help appears.
Someone gives him food.
It is a boy not much older than he is, dressed in an adult’s clothes, with a hat that threatens to fall off, with an extraordinarily assured manner: Jack Dawkins, the Artful Dodger.
He takes Oliver somewhere.
There is an old man, a group of boys, and handkerchiefs hanging from a line.
The old man is genial. He feeds Oliver, lets him sleep, and jokes with him.
The next essay examines that room and a change of position.
At the workhouse Oliver was a liability. Here he becomes something useful.
And usefulness, in this place, has a price.

articles.title: Fagin’s Lesson
articles.deck: Food, shelter, companions and praise are real. So are deception, confinement and the price of belonging.
body: Oliver is close to starving when he reaches the outskirts of London.
The Artful Dodger feeds him.
The boy is little older than Oliver, wearing an adult’s coat with rolled sleeves and a hat at an angle. He buys Oliver ham and bread, and gives him an alcoholic drink.
Come with me, he says. I know an old gentleman who will let you stay without charging you.
Oliver follows.
## The room
It is dirty and dark.
An old man toasts sausages at the fire. Boys smoke and drink at a table. Silk handkerchiefs hang from a line.
The old man is very friendly.
Fagin bows, shakes Oliver’s hand, and says he is pleased to meet him. He supplies food, drink, and a place to sleep.
The boys gather around and joke with him.
Oliver eats and sleeps better than he has for a long time.
## The lesson
The next morning, he watches a game.
Fagin walks about with a snuffbox, pocketbook, watch, spectacles, and handkerchief distributed about his person.
The Dodger and another boy follow him.
Their task is to remove each object without his noticing.
When they succeed, he laughs and praises them.
Oliver enjoys watching. It seems an amusing game.
Fagin later invites him to try. He takes a handkerchief from Fagin’s pocket.
Fagin pats his head and predicts that he will be as accomplished as the Dodger.
## More than deception
Pause here. It is often said that Fagin deceives Oliver.
He certainly does.
He describes the stolen goods as fine workmanship and encourages Oliver to think he can learn to make handkerchiefs. The boy does not understand what the game is preparing him for.
But lies alone do not explain the lesson’s power. Real provisions accompany the deception, drawing an uninformed child closer one step at a time.
First: food.
After seven days of hunger and walking, the Dodger is the first person in this new world to treat him kindly.
Second: somewhere to stay.
A nine-year-old with nowhere to go is given a bed.
Third: companions.
This matters most. Oliver has scarcely known acceptance. The workhouse counts him; the undertaker puts him beneath the counter; Noah bullies him.
At Fagin’s, boys joke with him, teach him to play, and treat him as one of their own.
Fourth: praise.
When he removes the handkerchief, Fagin pats his head and tells him he has a future.
For Oliver, praise is something almost unknown.
## What does Fagin want?
Fagin understands the account behind these four gifts.
He is cultivating instruments.
The novel later makes the business plain. The boys steal for him. He receives the goods and provides their maintenance.
It is a commercial arrangement.
Its crucial step is not merely teaching them to steal.
It is making other destinations harder to reach.
Watch how that happens.
Once a child participates in theft, exposure becomes a threat. Reporting to the authorities may expose his own involvement. His former home may not welcome him; elsewhere, nobody will vouch for him.
More importantly, Fagin knows about him while he knows little about Fagin.
Fagin therefore keeps the boys by more than locked doors.
He also makes them feel that outside there is nowhere to stand.
## Oliver’s first outing
Oliver first goes out with the Dodger and Charley Bates.
He does not know what they intend.
At a bookstall, he sees the Dodger put a hand into an elderly gentleman’s pocket.
For a moment he stands astonished. Then he understands.
Terrified, he runs.
The running boy is taken for the thief.
The gentleman cries for pursuit. People join in. Oliver is knocked down, struck, and taken to the magistrate.
This is one of the novel’s sharpest episodes.
Of the three boys, Oliver is the one who has not participated in the theft.
The Dodger and Bates escape, joining the cries to catch the thief.
The boy who fled in horror is captured.
The crowd is sure it has the right person.
The evidence seems simple: he ran.
## The elderly gentleman
The gentleman is Mr. Brownlow.
One opening in the case is that Brownlow himself is unsure.
He admits that seeing the boy run led him to pursue. He cannot be certain Oliver took the handkerchief, and asks the magistrate for leniency.
The magistrate will not properly listen.
Fang is bad-tempered and arbitrary. He cuts Brownlow short and sentences Oliver to three months’ hard labor.
The bookstall keeper supplies the evidence that saves him.
He arrives to explain that Oliver stood by while another boy took the handkerchief.
Someone who does not know Oliver speaks about what he has actually seen.
He almost fails to get a hearing: Fang rebukes him and initially orders him away.
He insists on speaking.
Oliver is released.
## A few days with Brownlow
Brownlow takes him home.
These are among the happiest days Oliver has known.
He falls ill and is cared for. He has a clean bed, food, people who speak kindly to him, new clothes, and books.
The significance of that interlude emerges in what follows.
Fagin’s circle finds him.
Nancy and Sikes seize him in the street.
Nancy embraces him, calling him her brother, and tells the crowd that he is a naughty runaway whom she has finally found.
To the bystanders, this looks like a welcome recovery: a sister has located her missing brother.
Nobody intervenes for Oliver.
He is dragged away.
## The second half of Fagin’s lesson
Back in the den, another part of the lesson begins.
They mock Oliver’s new clothes, make him change into his old ones, and take the new suit away.
Brownlow bought those clothes. He also entrusted Oliver with a five-pound note to pay a bookseller four pounds ten shillings and bring back the change.
The note is taken and ends up with Sikes. The clothes are put into Fagin’s keeping.
The effect reaches beyond taking his possessions: it makes Oliver appear a thief to Brownlow.
From Brownlow’s side, a trusted boy has gone out with money, books, and new clothes, then disappeared.
That is exactly what Fagin wants.
He does lock Oliver up.
He also works to close the route back.
Alongside confinement and violence, there is the effort to make the people outside believe that the child is a thief.
As we have seen, a lock is not the only thing that keeps someone inside. The fear of having no place outside can hold them there too.
Fagin locks doors and dismantles bridges.
## Two accounts beside one another
Put the first two essays together.
The workhouse counts Oliver as a liability.
A head, a portion of gruel, a negative entry to be removed for five pounds: in that account, he costs money.
With Fagin, he becomes useful.
What does Fagin see in him? A clean-looking child with an innocent face, who might pass for someone from a respectable home.
That appearance has a use.
A boy who looks like a little gentleman is valuable to thieves. He can avoid suspicion, enter respectable places, and disarm strangers.
Later, Sikes wants his small body for a different reason: it will fit through the window of a house he plans to rob.
On this side, Oliver is an excellent instrument.
The relation between the two sides is the point.
The workhouse calculates him as a liability and tries to remove him.
After removal, he lands somewhere that calculates him as an asset.
Useless and useful can lie only a street apart.
The accounting form is shared.
## Fagin is not a supernatural devil
One problem in this character must not be passed over.
Dickens writes Fagin through the anti-Jewish prejudices of his society.

Repeatedly naming him by his Jewishness, and using stock associations of appearance, greed, and degradation, the novel draws on antisemitic stereotypes. Dickens later altered some of this language after criticism.
That is a serious defect, not something the interpretation should excuse.
It does not prevent us from examining the character’s construction.
Reducing him to someone who enjoys evil explains too little.
He conducts business and manages risk, sending the children out rather than doing their work himself. His pet names and moments of attachment need not all be sheer performance.
What is most frightening is that food, shelter, companions, and praise are real.
In some immediate respects, the boys receive more there than the workhouse would give them.
And the provision has a price.
## Next
Another person belongs to that room.
Her name is Nancy.
She lives with Sikes and has been under Fagin’s influence since childhood. She says she began stealing before she was half Oliver’s age and has continued for twelve years.
She is the woman who embraces Oliver in the street, calls him her brother, and helps drag him back.
Her role in the kidnapping is crucial.
A man pulling away a screaming child might invite intervention. Her performance as a sister gives the crowd a reason not to interfere.
She knows what she is doing.
The next essay turns to her.
It begins by refusing to erase that participation.

articles.title: She Is an Accomplice
articles.deck: Nancy helps recapture the child. Her history and her later intervention do not cancel that participation.
body: Oliver is captured in the street and taken back.
The woman who embraces him, weeping and calling him her brother, is Nancy.
She tells the crowd that he has run away, that the family is frantic, that she has finally found him. She performs the part well.
The onlookers believe her.
Some even rebuke Oliver for distressing his sister.
Then Sikes appears, takes hold of his collar, and drags him away.
## She knows what she is doing
We must begin firmly here. This character is too easily softened into innocence.
Nancy participates.
She embraces Oliver and calls him her brother, presenting an abduction as a family taking its child home. Her performance makes a difference.
She is crucial to the kidnapping.
A man dragging a screaming boy down the street might provoke intervention. A sister collecting a runaway brother supplies an acceptable explanation.
She provides the story that allows everyone else to stand aside.
And she knows where Oliver is being taken.
She knows Fagin’s business, the dangers facing his boys, and what it means to put a child with a newly opened route to safety back into that room.
She does it nonetheless.
## Other things she does
It is not her only involvement.
She has long worked within Fagin’s operation.
After Oliver’s arrest, she also goes to the police office for information. She initially refuses. Sikes and Fagin alternate threats, promises, and inducements until she agrees.
She changes her appearance and eventually goes, convincingly performing the anxious search for a relative. The pressure she experiences does not make her participation disappear.
She steals.
She drinks.
Her first appearance is with Bet at Fagin’s rooms, where they subsequently drink.
She is an established, useful part of his world.
## Where she comes from
Now consider her history.
Dickens gives it briefly, and its few sentences carry enormous weight.
She says she began stealing before she was half Oliver’s age and has lived that way for twelve years.
Her childhood belongs beside those of the Dodger, Bates, and Oliver. She has simply been in that world much longer.
She has grown from a child thief into someone able to act a part, keep watch, and obtain information at the police office.
At one point she puts it bluntly.
The streets have been her home.
She has been cold and hungry there since childhood, and there she remains.
Another home has scarcely been imaginable to her.
## Nancy and Sikes
The man beside her is Bill Sikes.
In the contrast this essay draws, he is the novel’s most unqualified brute.
Fagin calculates his business. Sikes lashes out, robs, and kills. His violence toward his dog makes the animal fear him, yet it continues to follow.
He also beats Nancy.
The narrative presents violence as part of the ordinary conditions of their relationship.
She stays with him.
When she is urged to leave, her attachment becomes unmistakable.
He is the man to whom she is bound.
She describes both her feeling for him and the grip of the old life, as something from which she cannot simply turn away.
## The thing she cannot bear
Yet there is a line within this person, and that is the subject here.
After years in this world, she cannot bear what is happening to Oliver.
Why?
The distinction is particular.
Oliver has not yet been made into a thief.
The Dodger and Bates already take pride in their skill. Bates will later reform, but at this moment Oliver has not reached the position they occupy.
He is different.
Dragged back, he still cries, struggles, and hopes to return to Brownlow. He has not accepted what they accept.
Nancy sees something of her own childhood in him.
She tells Fagin and Sikes, in one of the novel’s most powerful speeches, what this life has meant.
She has stolen for twelve years, since she was a very small child. The cold streets have been her home, and the man who put her there has kept her at this work by day and night.
She condemns herself for helping bring the boy back.
## Taking him to Sikes
Later, Oliver is taken on a burglary.
Sikes needs his small body to enter through a window.
Nancy has previously shielded him from a beating.
When she comes to collect him, she says she has done all she can and shows him bruises on her neck and arms.
She nevertheless takes him to Sikes. She does not take part in the housebreaking itself. While trying to comfort the boy, she is still delivering him into danger.
The burglary fails. Oliver is shot and subsequently abandoned.
The household he was forced to enter takes him in: Mrs. Maylie and Rose.
Nancy does not then know where he is.
## Listening in secret
Monks appears.
He is tied to Oliver’s hidden family history. We eventually learn that he is Oliver’s half-brother on his father’s side and wants to destroy him for the sake of an inheritance.
He bargains with Fagin: money in return for turning Oliver into a genuine criminal, someone whose future can be ruined.
Nancy overhears.
She listens on separate occasions and pieces together the scheme.
Then she acts.
She drugs Sikes with laudanum, waits for him to sleep, and goes out alone.
## The hotel meeting
She seeks Rose.
Their meeting takes place at a hotel.
A woman from the lowest reaches of London enters a young gentlewoman’s room. Nancy trembles and hesitates at the threshold.
Rose asks her to sit.
She will not.
Then she tells her story.
She explains Monks, the bargain, and the plan to ruin Oliver. She has listened and remembered, and gives the information coherently.
She also says something about herself.
She helped bring Oliver back to Fagin.
She does not make herself innocent in the telling.
## The refusal
The next part is where this character becomes most difficult.
Rose wants her to stay.
She offers help, urging her to leave the dangerous place and find a safe home.
That concern begins before Nancy has supplied the whole story. Rose has not yet met Brownlow. His later offer at the bridge belongs to another meeting.
A route away is being offered to her.
She refuses.
Why?
The next essay will consider that question.
For now, the important point is that she has not made her own rescue a condition of helping the boy.
## She does not bargain with it
Consider the account.
She helps a child who has no family claim upon her.
Oliver is neither her relative nor a close friend. Their time together has been brief, and she is one of the people who deceived and captured him.
She does not demand a benefit for herself if his rescue succeeds.
Rose thanks her and wants to help. Nancy nevertheless intends to return to Fagin and Sikes’s world, with its old dangers.
She understands the risk of what she is doing.
She trembles and repeatedly insists that Rose must not follow her, investigate her, or reveal her part in the disclosure.
She proposes a place and time for contact: London Bridge, between eleven and midnight on Sunday nights.
Discovery could cost her her life at Sikes’s hands.
She goes ahead.
## Next
At the next meeting, Rose brings Brownlow to learn more about Monks.
Nancy comes as arranged.
This time Fagin has someone follow her.
It is Noah, the former undertaker’s apprentice who bullied Oliver and has since come to London and joined Fagin.
He follows her to the bridge and hides near the steps to listen.
He reports to Fagin.
Fagin tells Sikes.
The final essay examines that night.
It also returns to the refusal: Nancy could accept help, yet goes back.
She speaks of love and of a life that holds her fast. Those words do not finish explaining the decision for us.

articles.title: She Went Back
articles.deck: Compassion, attachment, a refused payment, and an act that does not wait to be settled by a new position.
body: Rose asks Nancy to stay.
At the hotel, she urges her to leave danger for a safe place. Later, at London Bridge, Brownlow explicitly offers arrangements for a life far away, even abroad.
The offers are sincere, not idle assurances.
Between those meetings, Rose has met Brownlow. Together they can provide resources and assistance, and want to open a way out.
Nancy refuses.
## What she says
She gives several reasons. Each leaves something difficult for her listeners to understand.
One concerns her sense of degradation.
She feels too deeply involved, beyond recovery, and fears bringing trouble upon the people offering help.
Rose will not accept the past as a reason to abandon her.
There is also fear.
Nancy fears discovery and fears bringing destruction upon people to whom she remains attached.
The proposed refuge, and later the offer of another country, could reduce the danger. They cannot instantly dissolve the old life’s grip.
The deepest attachment is to Sikes.
She intends to return to him.
Asked why, she describes how a woman without family or friends can make one man the center of her life.
She speaks of her feelings and of being entangled in the life she knows. She is not without reasons, though those reasons remain difficult to accept.
She even says she will return knowing that he might kill her.
## Why the refusal is difficult
Pause over this refusal. Few moments in the book resist explanation more strongly.
Two familiar readings seem insufficient.
The first is that she loves Sikes irrationally.
That assigns the matter to love, after which explanation can stop: love has no reasons, so obscurity is expected.
But stopping there leaves her recent conduct unexplained.
She has disclosed the associates’ scheme, reporting Fagin and Monks while Sikes sleeps under a drug she has given him.
Her attachment has not extinguished her judgment or her opposition to what they intend for the child.
The second reading is that her environment has destroyed her ability to choose anything else.
Taken to its limit, that reading makes her wholly incapable of action.
Yet she has just performed one of the novel’s most resourceful interventions.
She overhears conversations, assembles the clues, drugs Sikes, and crosses London alone to meet a stranger. She explains the scheme clearly and arranges another time and place for contact.
The act requires planning, judgment, and courage.
Her power to act has not been completely erased.
## What else can the refusal mean?
I propose another aspect: she does not want helping the child to become a bargain for a new life of her own.
Look at what Rose and Brownlow offer across the two meetings.
Money, arrangements, a safe place, a chance to begin again.
They are offered to Nancy.
They come from people in the respectable world who had not previously known her.
Why do they offer them?
Not simply because she has done a good deed. Rose is already willing to help this suffering woman before the full information is disclosed.
Later, Rose appeals to Nancy’s rescue of the child and capacity for repentance, but also explicitly says her concern is not only a reward for the information.
That compassion must not be erased.
What I want to examine is another form within the persuasion: a person performs a worthy act and is consequently judged fit for a new place.
Nancy has long lived within a version of that form.
She entered Fagin’s world as a small child. Her place there depends on her usefulness: watching, acting, obtaining information.
She is allowed to stay because she performs well.
Now the appeal to leave also includes the thought that she has saved a child and begun to repent.
This does not make Rose’s conduct equivalent to Fagin’s. It suggests that the pattern of “what you have done, and therefore what you deserve” can appear again under very different intentions.
The judges, standards, and proposed benefits have changed. The question is whether Nancy’s act must be settled by any of them.
## An act she does not put up for exchange
Helping Oliver was not conditional upon securing a reward for herself.
Notice her insistences throughout.
She does not want money.
She refuses payment because money is not why she came. Later, however, she asks Rose for a small personal keepsake and accepts her handkerchief.
She asks for secrecy: no following her, no investigating her, no public disclosure of what she has done.
At the bridge, Brownlow wants to locate Fagin. Nancy will not hand him over. After receiving a promise not to pursue him without her agreement, she continues supplying clues about Monks.
She draws that boundary.
She will not deliver those people up.
They have harmed her and also make up the life she knows. Saving the boy is not, for her, permission to surrender every former associate.
That does not make them innocent. It means her decision does not follow every step her helpers would prefer.
Consider the direction of these limits.
She will carry the disclosure this far, and no further.
She tells the scheme for the child’s sake, not in exchange for payment, public praise, or the arrest of all her old companions. Accepting a handkerchief does not put a price on the information.
She does not offer the act as a commodity.
## Why return?
“I will go back to him” can be read as another part of that refusal.
On this reading, disclosure immediately followed by a new life could too easily be narrated as an exchange.
She gives information; the good people give a future.
The account appears settled.
Her refusal interrupts that settlement.
Recall her admission that she helped bring Oliver back.
She does not erase her responsibility.
I would not read what follows only as atonement, as if a good deed canceled a bad deed and reduced the balance to zero.
After helping, she returns to the man who will kill her and to the danger of her former life.
The act has not produced a monetary return for her.
## Reasons that do not settle an account
Nancy speaks of attachment, fear, and the people with whom her life is bound up.
Those reasons can be heard without turning them into a table of gains and losses from which someone else calculates her proper choice.
What she does is not an account closed by payment.
She still goes back. Her attachment is real, and so is her judgment that the child must be helped. She has not arranged the two into an answer that satisfies other people.
Her explanations do not make the refusal easy to understand.
An act not aimed at reward can have reasons without those reasons being convertible into profit.
## That night
Noah follows her.
At the second meeting, she comes to London Bridge. He hides near the steps and listens.
He reports to Fagin.
Fagin passes the story to Sikes.
The manner of its telling is especially sinister.
He first works Sikes into a fury, building the threat before fully identifying Nancy’s part.
Sikes rushes away.
Fagin calls after him not to be too violent.
He immediately explains his concern in terms of safety: cunning rather than recklessness. Even his restraint contains a calculation for himself.
## Her death
Sikes returns and locks the door.
Nancy wakes.
Seeing his face, she asks in terror what has happened.
She does not escape.
She clings to him.
She grasps his clothes, begs for her life, and urges him to repent. There is still time: they can leave and live better lives far apart, never seeing each other again.
He still has time to turn back.
While pleading for herself, she also points toward a future in which he need not carry out the killing.
He strikes her.
He hits her twice with the butt of his pistol. Bleeding, she struggles to raise the handkerchief Rose gave her and offers a final prayer.
He kills her with a club.
## Sikes afterward
The novel follows him.
He runs.
He cannot get away.
Before pursuit catches up, he is already pursued by his own mind.
Wherever he goes, he seems to see Nancy’s eyes. Darkness, solitude, and sleep become intolerable.
He throws himself into fighting a fire, working desperately because activity briefly interrupts the images.
His dog follows. He tries to kill it because it could identify him.
The dog escapes.
Eventually he is cornered on a roof. Attempting to lower himself by a rope, he sees those eyes again, loses his balance, and is hanged by the rope caught around his neck.
The dog leaps and falls to its death.
## What does this ending explain?
Dickens gives Sikes’s flight considerable space. This essay reads it as more than retribution.
It makes something visible.
The person who finally kills Sikes is not a judge or one of his pursuers.
His own terrified mind contributes to his death.
In this reading, Nancy’s last moments are part of what gives the pursuing eyes their power.
Had she offered only curses and hatred, perhaps he could have forced the act into a story of two people injuring one another.
Instead, even as she clings to him, she says he can still turn back.
A man who believes himself betrayed hears the person before him begging to survive and still urging him away from destruction.
He cannot put that encounter into a form he can bear.
The eyes follow him.
## In closing
Bring the four essays together.

A nine-year-old asks for more gruel and causes an institutional crisis. The portion has already been calculated, and the calculation has no column for his hunger. The board need not personally hate him. It is managing expenditure.
A five-pound offer is made to remove a liability. The parish, not the person taking him, pays.
Then he reaches a place where he is an asset. Food, shelter, companions, and praise are real, and they come at a price.
Useless and useful lie close together. Both can belong to the same way of accounting for a person.
Yet one person’s action cannot be fully contained by that calculation.
She is an accomplice. She is the woman who deceived the crowd and helped take the child away. She acknowledges it herself.
She brings the information out without making money or a new life the condition, refuses to hand over every old companion, and wants her identity kept secret.
Others sincerely want to help and also speak in the language of redemption and worthiness. Her intervention does not wait to be settled by a better position.
She refuses the offered departure.
She describes her attachments, yet still leaves the others struggling to understand why she must return.
After returning, she is murdered.
Her act has earned her nothing in money.
The novel’s calculable things, the ration, the five-pound reward, the usefulness of a small body, all find their places in an account.
That act does not.
